p: Abby walked Jordan through the airspace over Denver, layer by layer, and the shelf whose floor sits at eight thousand feet right above Centennial.
Jordan learned the radios, canceled again for wildfire smoke, and kept Russ out of the fire's flight restriction by posting the notice in the club chat.
When the radio died near home, she landed on light signals from the tower.
Then on a clear Saturday, looking at the reservoir, she climbed to seventy eight hundred feet, just under the shelf, until Abby touched the altimeter.
In Danny's notebook she found he'd made the same climb years ago and gone through the floor, and she wrote her own rule on her kneeboard.
Claire Reyes. Danny's widow, who watched the June storm from her kitchen with Jordan.
Abby Strand. Jordan's instructor, and a stickler for the math.
Marisol Tran. The mechanic, and a partner in the club.
Ellie Reyes. Danny's daughter, who wanted to know why clouds are flat on the bottom.
Walt Herrera. The safety officer, still not sure about Jordan.
Russ Kim. The fourth partner, usually traveling.

The first week of August, Aurora ran out of shade. Jordan worked a Monday shift that started at seven in the morning with a roofer who'd stopped sweating, and her last call ended at three the next morning with a man in his eighties who'd fallen asleep in his garage with the door down and a box fan blowing hot air at him. Somewhere in the middle her partner said the truck's thermometer read 101, and neither of them laughed, because they'd already been to two of those calls and were about to go to a third.

Heat is a protocol. You cool them, you watch the pressure, you don't let them stand up too fast. She'd done it a hundred times. What she'd never done was think about what the same afternoon did to a 1978 Cessna sitting on the ramp at Centennial with its wings in the sun.
Tuesday night, slept out and showered, she was eating cold noodles on the couch when Claire called. Claire didn't call. Claire texted, in full sentences, with periods.

Ellie wants to go up in the airplane, Claire said, without saying hello. She's been asking since she was six. Danny always said when she's tall enough. She measured herself on the pantry door last night. She marked it with a Sharpie. A pause. Jordan could hear the dishwasher running on the other end. If Abby flies it. If you're in it. And if she goes, I go. That's the deal.
Jordan put the noodles down. Okay.
Saturday the fifteenth. I'm on days all week. Three o'clock is the only time I've got. Another pause. Don't make it a thing. I'll change my mind.
After she hung up Jordan sat there for a while. Then she texted Abby, and the answer came back before she'd set the phone down.

A text from Abby Strand. I can do the 15th at 3. Four of us, August, 3 in the afternoon. You're going to do the numbers. All of them. Thursday 8am, briefing room. Bring Biscuit's POH from the seat back and a pencil.

Wednesday she drove to the airport after her nap and got the POH out of the seat back pocket. Biscuit was tied down in her spot on the ramp with the sunshade in the windshield and the yoke lock in, and the cabin was hotter than the back of the ambulance. The book was soft at the corners, held together with clear packing tape along the spine. Section 5 was the most worn. On the takeoff distance page somebody had drawn a pencil box around the 8,000 foot row in the 2,300 pound block, and written next to it in small block capitals: THIS IS AUGUST.
She knew whose capitals those were.
Abby's Ground School: what the heat takes away.
Pressure altitude: start with the number the airplane feels.

Eight AM and the window unit's already losing. Sit. POH, Section 5, open, and it stays open. Everything today lives in there. So do half the performance questions on your written, because the FAA's favorite move is a chart, three numbers, and a stopwatch.

First number. Pressure altitude. Your altimeter's a barometer somebody painted feet on. It's set up for the standard atmosphere: 29.92 inches and 15°C at sea level, losing about 2°C a thousand feet. Local setting in the little window, it reads roughly your height above sea level. Put 29.92 in the window instead and it reads pressure altitude. That's height above the standard datum plane, a made up level where the pressure would be 29.92. The charts are built on that one.

Three ways to get it, per the PHAK. Twist 29.92 into the window and look. Use an E6B. Or the math, which is what I want from you. Field elevation, plus 29.92 minus the setting, times 1,000. Down low an inch of mercury is about a thousand feet, so a hundredth is about ten. This morning: 30.06. 29.92 minus 30.06, minus 0.14. Times 1,000, minus 140. 5,885 minus 140, 5,745. High pressure, the airplane thinks she's lower than she is. Low pressure, higher. The sign is where people bleed points on the written. Get it backward and you can get it backward with total confidence.
Write the pressure altitude down before anything else. Every chart in that section wants it, and none of them want your field elevation.

How the exam asks it. Expect to compute pressure altitude from an elevation and an altimeter setting. A setting above 29.92 gives a pressure altitude below field elevation. A setting below 29.92 gives one above it.
Density altitude, and why August is a different airport.

Pressure altitude assumes the standard temperature. It's August. The temperature is not standard. Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature, and it's the altitude in the standard atmosphere where the air would be as thin as the air you've actually got. The PHAK says it in one sentence I want you to remember: regardless of the actual altitude, the airplane performs as though it were operating at the density altitude.

The rule of thumb is density altitude equals pressure altitude plus 120 times the difference between the outside air temperature and the standard temperature at that pressure altitude. Standard temperature is 15 minus 2 for every thousand feet. At 6,000 feet that's 15 minus 12, or 3°C. Three degrees. That's what standard is up here. Today's forecast high is 34. So at our pressure altitude this afternoon, call it about 5,900, standard is about 3, the real air is 31 degrees hotter than that, and 31 times 120 is about 3,700 feet. Add it on, and Biscuit is going to take off from Centennial feeling like she's at about 9,600 feet. She's never seen 9,600 feet in her life without almost four thousand feet of climbing first.

The common mistake is using 15°C as the standard temperature at every altitude. That's only true at sea level. Up here it'll make your density altitude look about 1,400 feet better than it is, and that's the wrong direction to be wrong.

High elevation, low pressure, high temperature, and high humidity all push density altitude up. Low elevation, high pressure, cold, and dry pull it down. Humidity is the sneaky one. Water vapor is lighter than air, so moist air is less dense than dry air. There's no rule of thumb or chart for it, and the PHAK says humidity alone usually isn't a big factor, but it still costs you some performance, so when it's hot and sticky expect a little less than the chart says. We mostly don't have that problem in Colorado. We have the other three.

How the exam asks it. Know which conditions raise density altitude and that higher density altitude means worse performance. For the math, the standard temperature has to be computed at the pressure altitude, not left at 15°C.
What thin air does to the engine, the prop, and the wing.

The PHAK lists three things you lose. Power, because the engine takes in less air with every breath. Thrust, because the propeller has less air to bite. And lift, because thin air pushes on the wing with less force at any given speed.

Biscuit's engine has no supercharger, so it starts losing power the moment it leaves sea level, and it's already lost a lot of it sitting here. The mixture matters more than it does anywhere else. The carburetor was set up for sea level air, so at a high field full rich is too rich, and too rich at full throttle is less power. That's why the POH note says to lean for maximum RPM in a full throttle runup before takeoff from fields above 3,000 feet. You know this from Marisol's hangar. Today you're going to feel it.

Now the wing, which is where people get confused. The wing needs the same dynamic pressure as always, so she lifts off at her usual indicated airspeed. Fine. But in thin air that indicated number comes with a bigger true airspeed, so more groundspeed when the wheels leave. You need more speed and you've got less engine to make it with. The airspeed indicator looks totally normal. The runway edge lights go by like you're on I-25. Landing's the same deal in reverse. Same indicated numbers, more speed over the concrete at touchdown, longer rollout.

Climb hurts worst. Climb is excess power: what's left after you've paid the bill for staying level. Thin air cuts your paycheck and leaves the bill alone. Absolute ceiling, nothing left, zero feet a minute. Service ceiling, 100 feet a minute and no better. Both of Biscuit's got a lot lower since breakfast.

How the exam asks it. At high density altitude the airplane lifts off and lands at the same indicated airspeed but a higher true airspeed and groundspeed. Takeoff roll goes up, climb rate goes down, landing roll goes up.

Now the page with the pencil box on it. Biscuit's takeoff table is a short field table, which means the numbers assume the short field technique in the book, flaps up, full throttle before you let off the brakes, on a paved, level, dry runway with no wind. Weight picks the block, pressure altitude picks the row, temperature picks the column. Each box has two numbers, ground roll and total distance over a 50 foot obstacle, and the second one's the one that keeps you out of the trees.

Read the conditions line at the top of every chart before you read a single number in it. The PHAK warns that manufacturers don't present this stuff the same way. Some charts are built on pressure altitude, some on density altitude, some are tables and some are graphs, and the numbers mean nothing if you put the wrong thing in.

When your conditions land between rows or columns, you interpolate. That just means if you're halfway between two numbers, you take the number halfway between them. If you're 40 percent of the way from 30°C to 40°C, you go 40 percent of the way from the 30 degree distance to the 40 degree distance. Weight and pressure altitude, I want you to round up to the next block and the next row instead of interpolating. Up, always, toward the worse number. And a chart is a test pilot in a new airplane on a good day. Biscuit is 48 years old and you're a student. That's what the ACS means when it asks about differences between calculated and actual performance.

Then the notes under the table, which are the part people skip. Ours say three things. Lean for max RPM at full throttle before takeoff above 3,000 feet. Decrease the distances 10 percent for each 9 knots of headwind, and for tailwinds up to 10 knots, increase them 10 percent for each 2 knots. And on a dry grass runway, add 15 percent of the ground roll figure. Look at those wind numbers again. See it? Headwind gives you a little back. Tailwind takes a lot more away. The PHAK says the same thing in general terms: a headwind that's 10 percent of your takeoff speed cuts the distance about 19 percent, and a tailwind that's 10 percent of your takeoff speed adds about 21 percent. Upslope runways are longer for takeoff. Downslope runways are shorter for takeoff and longer for landing, and the Chart Supplement tells you the slope. Grass, slush, snow, and standing water all add distance. A wet runway adds landing distance for a reason that has a name, hydroplaning, where the tires ride up on a film of water and stop doing anything useful. The PHAK puts the speed where it can start at about nine times the square root of the tire pressure. Thirty six psi, square root six, times nine, about 54 knots. And once it starts, the brakes do almost nothing. Land as slowly as you safely can, and don't count on stopping where you'd stop on a dry day.

My own rule, and it's mine, not the FAA's: take the corrected distance over 50 feet and add half again. If that number doesn't fit the runway, we don't go. 91.103 says you have to know your runway lengths and your takeoff and landing distance data before every flight. It doesn't say how much room to leave. I do.

Here's what the ACS means by pilot technique. The book's numbers came from a test pilot who did everything exactly right: power up smoothly, rotation speed right on the number, climb speed held to the knot. Rotate late and you use more runway. Rotate early and she drags herself along nose high with the drag up, which is worse. Hold the nose too high after liftoff and you climb slower than the chart thinks. Landing is where technique costs the most. Every knot of excess airspeed over the fence turns into float, and float is runway you never get back. Touchdown speed matters too. Land fast and the brakes have more to do. So the chart is the best you'll ever see, and your technique decides how far short of it you fall.

Then the flaps. The numbers are only yours if Biscuit's set up the way she was when Cessna made them. Biscuit's book says flaps up for a normal takeoff and flaps up for the short field takeoff this table was built on. Ten degrees is for the shortest ground roll or a soft or rough field, so the wing lifts the weight off the wheels sooner and drags you out of the mud. Nothing past 10 is approved for takeoff, and the book says skip the 10 over an obstacle when it's high and hot. That's Centennial in July. Trim set for takeoff, every time, or she fights you at rotation. Cowl flaps, on anything that has them, are open for takeoff. Hot engine otherwise. Set what the book says for this takeoff, and read the chart for this takeoff, not the one next to it.
How the exam asks it. Expect a table or graph, a set of conditions, and a wind correction from the chart notes. Read the conditions line first. Headwind credit is small and tailwind penalty is large.

You can't do much about the weather. You can do a lot about weight. The PHAK has a list of what too much weight costs you, and it's long. Higher takeoff speed. Longer takeoff run. Worse climb rate and climb angle. Lower ceiling, shorter range, slower cruise. Higher stall speed. Faster approach. Longer landing roll. And it says the first sign that an airplane's overloaded usually shows up during the takeoff.

Here's the part that should scare you a little. A heavier airplane needs more lift to leave the ground, so it needs more speed. The PHAK says a 21 percent increase in weight takes a 10 percent increase in lift-off speed. And because distance goes with the square of speed and the extra mass also slows the acceleration, a 10 percent increase in takeoff weight costs you at least a 21 percent increase in takeoff distance. Landing is gentler on paper. A 10 percent heavier airplane needs about 10 percent more landing distance. But a 10 percent fast approach, at any weight, costs you at least 21 percent more landing distance. Wind works the same way it does on takeoff: a tailwind that's 10 percent of your landing speed adds about 21 percent, and at our approach speeds a 10 knot tailwind is more than that. Landing distance also grows about 3.5 percent for every thousand feet of altitude, which is about 20 percent before you've even left our ramp.

Now the legal side. Maximum weight is an operating limitation, and 91.9 says nobody operates an aircraft without complying with the operating limitations in its flight manual, markings, and placards. For a 172N that's 2,300 pounds in the normal category. It's on the type certificate. The PHAK also says something nobody puts on a bumper sticker: an airplane certified for a maximum weight may not be able to take off safely at that weight under all conditions. High, hot, and humid may require a reduction in weight before flight is attempted. The maximum is a ceiling, and on some days it's a ceiling you shouldn't get anywhere near.

One weight problem is really a where problem. Whatever goes in the airplane has to stay where you put it. Bags in the baggage compartment, under the placard number, strapped down to the rings in the floor or under the net. A loose bag in a steep climb slides aft and takes the CG with it. A loose bag on a hard landing comes forward into the back of your passenger's head. Loose items in the cabin are worse. I once watched a student chase a water bottle around the rudder pedals on short final. Don't be that student. Before engine start, look around like you're about to fly upside down. You aren't. Turbulence doesn't care.

How the exam asks it. Know the PHAK list of overweight effects and the classic percentages: 21 percent more weight needs 10 percent more lift-off speed, 10 percent more weight needs at least 21 percent more takeoff distance, 10 percent extra landing speed needs at least 21 percent more landing distance.
Balance: arms, moments, and the box you have to stay in.

Weight is how much. Balance is where. The center of gravity is the point the airplane would balance on if you could hang it from one string, and it has to be inside the CG limits the manufacturer set. Every location in the airplane is measured from a datum, which is just a reference line Cessna picked. For a 172N it's the lower front face of the firewall. The distance from the datum to an item is its arm, in inches, plus if it's behind the datum. Multiply weight by arm and you get its moment, in pound inches. Add up all the weights. Add up all the moments. Divide total moment by total weight, and that's your CG. That's the whole method. The PHAK walks through it with a table, and so do I.

Biscuit's numbers come from three places. The type certificate data sheet says the 172N seats sit two at 34 to 46 inches, which is why Biscuit's paperwork uses 37 for the front seats, and two at 73. Baggage is 120 pounds max at 95 inches. Fuel is 40 usable gallons at 48 inches, and usable fuel weighs 6 pounds a gallon. Her basic empty weight and its arm come from her own weight and balance report, the current one, in the airplane's records. Not the sample in the POH. The PHAK says sample loading problems are for guidance only, because every airplane gets modified and every airplane is different. Ours includes the unusable fuel and full oil, so you don't add those.

The CG range on the type certificate for a 172N is 35.0 to 47.3 inches at 1,950 pounds or less, and 38.5 to 47.3 inches at 2,300 pounds, with a straight line between them. So the aft limit stays put and the forward limit slides aft as the airplane gets heavier. That's the envelope. The POH draws that as a box with one corner cut off. Weight up the side, moment or CG along the bottom, make a dot. Dot's inside at takeoff and inside at landing or you don't go. Biscuit's fuel sits a few inches behind where her CG usually lives, so burning it slides the dot forward a little, about an inch at most. Plenty of airplanes move a lot more.

Dot's outside? Move something. The weight and balance handbook has one formula and you can flip it around for any unknown. Weight shifted over total weight equals change in CG over distance moved. Or the way I use it: CG change equals weight shifted, times distance, divided by total weight. Say a 190 pound guy moves from the back seat up front. That's 36 inches. Airplane weighs 2,286. 190 times 36 is 6,840, divided by 2,286, about 3 inches forward. Huge. People are the heaviest thing you get to move around.

How the exam asks it. Expect a loading problem: fill in weight, arm, and moment, total them, divide, and check the envelope. Expect a weight shift problem solved with the 8083-1B formula. Use 6 pounds per gallon for avgas.
Forward CG, aft CG, and how each one bites.

Biscuit's tail pushes down. Everybody's surprised by that. The CG normally sits a little ahead of the center of lift, so she wants to drop her nose, and the horizontal tail fights it by pushing down. Which means the wing is lifting the airplane plus whatever the tail's pushing.

Forward CG, the tail pushes harder. More load on the wing. The PHAK: stalls at a higher speed. More back pressure, and way up at the front of the range you can run out of elevator in the flare and land on the nosewheel, which Marisol will hear about. The forward limit's usually picked for landing. Forward is stable and heavy and a touch slow in cruise from the tail drag.

Aft CG means less tail download, so a little less drag and a little more cruise speed. That's the good news. The bad news? It's less stable. The control forces get light, which makes it easy to overstress the airplane by accident, and stall recovery gets harder. Spin recovery gets harder too, and far enough aft you can get a flat spin that won't recover. The PHAK says an airplane that recovers fine from a spin at one CG can fail to recover when the CG moves aft by an inch or two. Out of the two, aft of the limit is the one that kills people.

There's a second category on the type certificate for a reason. A 172N in the utility category has a lower weight, 2,000 pounds, and a much tighter aft limit, because utility maneuvers need it. We're in the normal category every day, and we stay there.
How the exam asks it. Know the forward and aft CG lists. Forward: higher stall speed. Aft: reduced stability and harder stall and spin recovery.
Climbing, ground effect, and the point where you quit.

Two climb speeds. VX, the best angle of climb speed, gets you the most altitude for the distance over the ground, which is what you want with trees at the end of the runway. VY, the best rate of climb speed, gets you the most altitude for the time, which is what you want the rest of the time. In a propeller airplane VX is slower than VY, and both are in the POH. The AFH says a 5 knot miss from either one can cost a lot of climb, so you fly them, not near them.

Ground effect is the trap. Get the wing close to the runway, within about one wingspan, and the ground squashes the wingtip vortices, so induced drag drops. A quarter of the span up, that's about 25 percent less induced drag. A tenth of the span, about half. Now picture a heavy airplane on a hot day. It lifts off below the speed it needs, floats along in ground effect feeling fine, then climbs out of it into thin air and the drag comes back all at once. The AFH says it plainly: at high density altitude, high temperature, or maximum weight, an airplane may lift off and not be able to climb out of ground effect. If that's you, don't pull. Lower the nose a little, stay in ground effect, let it accelerate to climb speed. Pulling is how people stall twenty feet off the runway.

Last thing, and it's the one I care about most. Before every takeoff, the AFH says to pick a point on the runway where you should be airborne. If you get there and you aren't, you pull the power to idle, brake, and keep it straight. One more thing from that chapter: the takeoff ground roll plus the landing ground roll from the POH is a good estimate of the runway you need to speed up and then stop. On a 10,000 foot runway it'll feel silly. Do it anyway. It's the habit you want the day you're somewhere with 4,000 feet and a fence.
And lean the thing, from the doorway. Marisol, coffee, no idea how long she's been there. Correct, though. Full rich at this elevation in August and you get to meet a much smaller engine.

How the exam asks it. Ground effect reduces induced drag near the surface, and an airplane lifted off too early may not climb out of it at high density altitude. Know VX versus VY, and the AFH advice to choose a point on the runway to be airborne by.
At 8:10 Abby wrote the morning's two lines on the whiteboard. The air conditioner in the briefing room window was running full blast and doing about as much good as a dog panting at the sun.

Centennial, Thursday, 6:53 AM. Wind one eight zero at four, ten miles, sky clear, seventeen and seven, altimeter thirty oh six. And the forecast for one in the afternoon, nineteen hundred Zulu: wind three three zero at ten, thirty four degrees Celsius, altimeter twenty nine ninety.
We're going to fly at one this afternoon, on purpose, in the heat, so you know what you're asking Biscuit for next Saturday. Pressure altitude at one o'clock. Show me how you got it.
Jordan had the POH open in front of her, the pencil box on the 8,000 foot row staring up at her.
Field elevation is 5,885, and the one o'clock altimeter forecast is 29.90. What's the pressure altitude?
A. 5,865. Subtract twenty feet from field elevation for the lower setting.
B. Set 29.90 in the window, and read the altimeter on the ramp.
C. About 5,885. The setting is close enough to 29.92 to skip the math.
D. 5,905. Add twenty feet to field elevation for the lower setting.

Fifty nine oh five. Twenty feet up, because the setting's low. Yep. Low pressure, the airplane thinks it's higher than it is. She writes 5,905 in the corner of the board in green marker and boxes it. Everything this afternoon starts from that box. Don't make me erase it.

That's it. Pressure altitude is field elevation plus the difference between 29.92 and the setting, times 1,000. 5,885 plus 20 is 5,905. A setting below 29.92 puts pressure altitude above field elevation.
Decision two. Thirty one degrees above standard.
Next. Density altitude, one o'clock, and then tell me what it means for us in real words. Not test words.
Jordan worked it on the legal pad. Standard temperature at 5,905 feet. Then the difference. Then times 120. She checked it twice like a drip rate, then once more because Abby was watching.
At 34 degrees Celsius and a 5,905 foot pressure altitude, what's the density altitude, and what does it mean?
A. About 9,600. The engine makes less power, but the wing works the same.
B. About 8,200, with 15°C as standard. Biscuit performs like she's at 8,200.
C. About 9,600. Biscuit will perform like she's up at 9,600 feet.
D. About 9,600. That's what the altimeter reads after takeoff.

About ninety six hundred. Yep. She writes it under the box. 9,600. Then she writes 5,885 next to it and draws a long arrow between them. Call it thirty seven hundred feet of mountain we never had to climb. Engine, prop, wing, all three of them think they're up there. The runway's the only thing still at 5,885.

Yep. That's the one. Standard at 5,905 is 15 minus 11.8, about 3.2 degrees. 34 minus 3.2 is 30.8. 30.8 times 120 is about 3,700. 5,905 plus 3,700 is about 9,600 feet. The airplane performs as though it's at the density altitude.

Tucked into the back of the POH, behind Section 6, was an index card in a plastic sleeve. Danny's capitals again. BISCUIT W&B. EMPTY 1,438 39.1. ME 185. FULL FUEL 240. Under that, a column of loading combinations he'd worked out and a smiley face next to the bottom one.
Jordan held it up. Abby didn't take it. Before you use anything on that card, go ask Marisol where she keeps the airplane's records. Then decide which empty weight you believe.
Marisol was at her bench in the hangar with a carburetor in pieces on a shop towel. She looked at the card, and something went across her face and came back.
Danny's card says Biscuit's empty is 1,438 at 39.1. Which number should Jordan trust?
A. The empty weight from the sample loading problem in the POH.
B. The latest weight and balance report in the maintenance records.
C. Danny's card, the same numbers he flew Biscuit on for years.
D. Danny's card, plus about twenty pounds for the radios and the GPS.

Marisol pulls a binder off the shelf over the bench and opens it to a tab marked W&B. On top is a form with her own signature on it, dated October 2019. ADS-B box, the panel GPS, the antenna, the wiring. I weighed her on scales after. 1,486 at 39.5. She looks at the card in Jordan's hand. That card's from before. He never redid it. I told him to. She closes the binder and hands it over. Forty eight pounds, she's gained. Same as Walt since 1978.

Exactly right. The current weight and balance record for this specific airplane is the only empty weight that counts. Equipment changes alter both weight and CG, and the PHAK says those changes must be recorded. An old card, even a careful one, describes an airplane that no longer exists.
Decision four. Two of us and forty gallons.

Back in the briefing room, with the binder, Abby slid the blank worksheet across the table. This afternoon. You, me, full tanks, our two flight bags and a gallon of water in the back, because it's August and I'm not dying of heatstroke over Bennett. Weight and balance. Go.
I'm one fifty with boots on. I'll say it once.
Jordan had a pencil in her hand and the urge, which she noticed and didn't like, to say two people is obviously fine.
Two people, full tanks, bags and water are on board this afternoon. How should Jordan do weight and balance?
A. Work the moment for each item and check the CG against the envelope.
B. Run the full worksheet with standard weights of 170 per person.
C. Skip the worksheet. Two people and full fuel always fit in a 172.
D. Total the weights and check the sum against the 2,300 pound limit.

She does it in pencil, in neat columns, the way she'd chart vitals. 2,058 pounds. 83,661 pound inches. 40.65. She checks the forward limit at that weight and gets 36.08. Inside, with room. Abby reads it upside down and doesn't say anything, which is how Jordan knows it's right. Then she says, Now keep that sheet. Saturday you'll add two people to it.

That's it. The computational method: list weight and arm, compute each moment, total the weights and moments, divide for CG, and check it against the limits at that weight. It takes four minutes and it's the only way to know.
Decision five. The page with the box on it.
Now the takeoff table. 2,058 pounds, 5,905 feet, 34 degrees. Tell me which numbers you're going to use and why.

Biscuit's POH, section five, short field takeoff distance. Flaps up, full throttle before brake release, a paved, level, dry runway, no wind. There are two weight blocks, twenty three hundred and twenty one hundred pounds, with rows for five, six, seven and eight thousand feet and columns for twenty, thirty and forty degrees Celsius, and each box gives the ground roll and the total to clear a fifty foot obstacle. Three notes: above three thousand feet, lean for max RPM before takeoff. Cut ten percent for each nine knots of headwind, and with a tailwind up to ten knots, add ten percent for each two knots. On dry grass, add fifteen percent of the ground roll.
In pencil, off to the side of the 8,000 foot row in the 2,300 pound block, was the box and the word AUGUST.
At 2,058 pounds, 5,905 feet and 34 degrees, which chart entries should Jordan use?
A. The 2,100 block at 6,000, but round 34 down to the 30°C column.
B. The 2,100 block at 5,000, entering the rows with field elevation.
C. The 2,300 block at 8,000 and 40°C, the worst box on the page.
D. The 2,100 block at 6,000, interpolating 34 between 30 and 40°C.

Why 2,100 and not 2,058? Jordan doesn't look up. Next heavier block. Round toward worse. And why interpolate the temperature? Jordan, still not looking up: Because thirty four's a real number and I've got it. Abby nods once and gets up to refill her coffee. The machine has smelled like burnt toast since Jordan's first lesson in April. Over her shoulder she says, Weight and altitude, round up. Temperature you can work. Now do the wind, and don't look at me while you do it, I'm not going to make a face. She makes a face anyway when Jordan writes cosine, but it's the good face, the one Jordan's seen maybe twice.

Yep. That's the one. Round weight and pressure altitude to the next more demanding entry, so 2,100 lb and 6,000 feet. Interpolate temperature proportionally: 34 degrees is 40 percent of the way from 30 to 40. Then apply the wind note.

At 12:50 the ramp was shimmering like a parking lot in a truck commercial, and it was only getting worse. The tie down ropes were hot enough that Jordan untied them with her sleeves pulled down over her hands, and when she got in, the yoke was too hot to hold, so she sat there with the door open and the little air vents blowing on it until she could. Somebody two rows over was washing a Bonanza and the water was drying on the wing before he could get the chamois to it. The ATIS said wind three two zero at one zero, temperature three four, altimeter two niner niner zero, runway three five right. She'd already turned the temperature into a density altitude on the legal pad in her lap.

The run up went fine. She leaned for max RPM at full throttle like the note said, and watched the tach climb as she did it, which was a strange thing to watch, a number getting better because she'd taken something away. At the hold short line, Abby said:
Before you go. Where do you quit?
A. At the far end, if they're still on the ground and not making power.
B. At the taxiway 1,500 feet down if they're still on the ground.
C. Wherever the airspeed starts to feel too slow to her on the roll.
D. Nowhere special. With ten thousand feet, there's room for anything.

The taxiway fifteen hundred feet down. If we're still on the ground there, I pull the power and stop. Good. Say it out loud on the roll. So she does. Throttle in, brakes off. Biscuit gets going like she's wading. Airspeed alive. Forty. Taxiway coming. Off before it by a few hundred feet. Jordan had wanted more.

Exactly right. The chart says about 1,050 feet of ground roll with the headwind, so 1,500 feet gives the airplane a fair chance and leaves more than 8,000 feet to stop. Choosing an abort point you can see, with plenty of runway left to stop, turns a vague worry into one decision you've already made. If you reach it on the ground, power to idle, brake, and stay straight.

Takeoff number two was off 35L, the short one, 7,000 feet, because Abby wanted Jordan to see a runway end that wasn't a rumor. Jordan pulled back early. Not by much. She knew it right away, same as she knew a missed IV before the flash chamber stayed empty. Biscuit lifted, then sat there five feet off the concrete like she was thinking it over. One chirp from the stall horn. The airspeed was two knots under the grease pencil tick Abby had put on the glass that morning, the one Marisol was going to gripe about cleaning off. Runway left, sure, plenty. Past that the fence, and a road, and a business park full of beige roofs cooking in the sun, and that was about it for options.
Abby's hands were in her lap. They stayed there.
Biscuit lifted off two knots slow and is floating just off the runway. What should Jordan do?
A. Lower the nose a little and build up speed before she climbs.
B. Ease back and get her climbing before the runway end gets closer.
C. Hold the attitude where it is and let her climb on her own.
D. Pull the power to idle, and put her back on the runway that's left.

Jordan puts the nose down about two degrees. She hates it. Some lizard part of her brain hates it for the full two seconds, and two seconds on that clock is about a week. The horn quits. The needle creeps up to the grease pencil. Then she lets the nose come up and Biscuit climbs out over the fence and the road and the business park, slow as anything, while some guy in a parking lot stops loading his truck to watch. Probably wondering if he should call somebody. Abby breathes out. Ground effect. Thirty six feet, give or take, about one wingspan. Then it's gone. You did fine. GE on the kneeboard, underlined twice. Nobody talks again until the reservoir, which is fine with Jordan.

That's it. Lifting off below the recommended speed at high density altitude can leave an airplane flying in ground effect but unable to climb out of it. The AFH fix is to lower the pitch, accelerate in ground effect to climb speed, here VX for the fence, then climb.

They climbed east to 7,500 under the shelf. It took a while. Abby had her time it, and it was about 520 feet a minute with just the two of them, which Jordan wrote on her kneeboard under the 5,905 and the 9,600, because she had a feeling she was going to want all three of those numbers again on Saturday. Out past the reservoir the plains were brown already, a month early, and the wheat that was left had been cut into stubble that threw heat up at them in bumps you could see coming only because the dust devils marked them. Over Bennett it got bumpy enough that her pencil came off the kneeboard twice. A water bottle rolled around the floor the whole lesson. Hers, probably.

On the way back in, somewhere over the reservoir, Abby said, Feel how much back pressure she wants? That's us two and a gallon jug. Saturday you've got Claire and Ellie back there instead of a jug. What changes?
A. The CG moves aft. That makes her more stable and steadier in pitch.
B. Not much. The rear seats are near the CG, so trim and feel stay put.
C. The CG goes aft. She'll be less stable, and lighter in pitch.
D. The CG goes aft, and her stall speed goes up with it.

The CG goes aft. She'll be less stable, and lighter in pitch. Yep. Also about a knot faster in cruise. Nobody at the club's ever noticed that, not even Russ, who'd spot a free knot from across the street. She taps the trim wheel between the seats with the toe of her boot. Today we're nose heavy, so you've been cranking in nose up trim all the way down final like you're winding a clock. Saturday, less. Trim it like today and she'll balloon on you right over the numbers with Claire watching.

Yep. That's the one. An aft CG reduces the tail's download. The airplane is less stable, control forces get lighter, stall and spin recovery gets harder, and cruise speed rises a little. A forward CG gives a higher stall speed and heavier elevator forces.

Sunday it was 97 in Parker and Claire's air conditioner was making a noise like a dentist's drill in the next room. The three of them ended up on the kitchen floor in front of the open freezer, eating grape popsicles, because Ellie said that was the rule over 95 and nobody could prove otherwise.
Ellie knew about Thursday. Ellie knew about all of it. Claire knew about all of it, from Abby, by text. Jordan filed that away to be weird about later.
Mom says Biscuit had a hard time getting up because it was hot. Ellie got the drip on the side of her popsicle with her tongue, mostly. Does the airplane get tired?

Over Ellie's head Claire gave Jordan a look. Her own popsicle was running down into her watchband and she wasn't doing a thing about it. It was the look from the trampoline in May, the clouds question. Your turn.
Ellie wants to know if Biscuit gets tired on hot days. What should Jordan tell her?
A. "No. Machines don't get tired if you take care of them."
B. "Kind of. Her engine gets too hot, and then she can't push as hard."
C. "Kind of. Hot air is thinner, so she has to work harder to fly in it."
D. "Kind of. Hot air weighs more, so she has more of it to lift."

Kind of. Hot air is thinner, so she has to work harder to fly in it. Ellie chews on that. Like when you run at the top of a mountain. Exactly like that. Same lungs, less air in every breath. Engine, propeller, wings, all of it runs on air, and on a 97 degree day there's less of it to go around. Ellie licks the stick, considering. So she's not tired. She's out of breath. Okay, that's better than how I said it. Ellie finishes the popsicle, very pleased with herself, and talks around the stick: Is she going to be out of breath on Saturday? Claire gets up and shuts the freezer. Then she just stands there with her back to them, a little too long.

Exactly right. Hot air is less dense. The engine makes less power, the propeller makes less thrust, and the wing makes less lift at a given true airspeed, so the airplane needs more runway and climbs slower. Out of breath is close to perfect.
Wednesday evening Walt was in the hangar when she came by, sitting on Marisol's stool with his glasses on the end of his nose and a sheet of paper on his knee. He didn't say hello. He held it out.
Russ is taking two guys from his softball team to Greeley Sunday morning for golf. He did his own numbers. He says they work. Check them.

Russ's loading sheet for Sunday. Empty, 1,486 pounds at 39.5. Russ up front at arm 37, 180. Mike and Dev in back at arm 73, 190 each. The clubs at 95, 120 pounds, and twenty gallons of fuel at 48, 120 more. Total 2,286 pounds, moment 110,257, and at the bottom, CG about 48, under gross, good to go, the guys like the back, more legroom.
Jordan did the division on her phone. 48.23. She opened the POH to the envelope. Aft limit 47.3, at every weight.
Russ's softball loading sheet is under gross weight. What should Jordan tell him?
A. Tell him to burn off some fuel first, and the CG will move forward.
B. Tell him to move one passenger up front, into the right seat.
C. Tell him he's fine to go. He's under max gross at 2,286.
D. Tell him to strap the golf bags into the empty front seat.

She shows Walt the work. 190 pounds times 36 inches, divided by 2,286. 2.99. New CG 45.24. Inside, with room. Walt reads it, then reads the division again. Send it to him. Not me. You. She does. Russ answers in four minutes: wait the back is NOT more legroom?? Then: ok dev sits up front. he's going to want the window. this is a nightmare. thank you. Walt stands up and puts the stool back where Marisol keeps it, exactly, and on his way out he says, That's three times now. She hadn't known he was counting.

That's it. The weight shift formula from the FAA's weight and balance handbook: the CG change is weight shifted times distance, divided by total weight. Here that's 190 times 36, divided by 2,286, or 2.99 inches. So 48.23 comes forward to 45.24, inside the 47.3 limit. The total doesn't change, only where it sits.

Thursday the 13th was hotter than the week before. Abby wanted one more hot takeoff before Saturday, then pattern work, then out. At the hold short Jordan did the run up and the mag check, and the radio got busy, and the tower cleared them for takeoff with a Citation on a three mile final.

Full throttle. Brakes off. Something was off. The tach was lower than last week. Not a lot. Maybe a hundred RPM, and with the tach reading fifty high to begin with, she didn't trust her own math. The airplane was rolling, just slowly. Her abort point, a taxiway she'd picked off the diagram, was coming up, and the airspeed needle was a long way from where it had been at that taxiway last Thursday.
Her eyes went to the red knob. All the way in. Full rich. She'd pushed it in for the mag check and never pulled it back.
The tach reads about a hundred RPM low, and her abort point is coming up. What should Jordan do?
A. Keep the power in and lean the mixture while she rolls.
B. Keep going. With ten thousand feet of runway she'll get off eventually.
C. Pull the carb heat on and keep the takeoff roll going.
D. Pull the power to idle and stop straight ahead on the runway.

Idle. Brakes. Nose dips. Centerline, mostly. She gets it off at the next taxiway with her pulse up where it lives on a three story carry down. Centennial Tower, Cessna Niner One Echo, rejected takeoff, clear of the runway. Tower says roger like she's asked for the time. On the taxiway she leans it out, full throttle, brakes on, and the tach comes up a hundred and twenty. She points at it. Abby nods. There you go. Screwed up, found out, still on the ground. That's the good version. Second try, they're off well before the taxiway.

Yep. That's the one. If the airplane isn't performing by the point you chose, reject the takeoff: power to idle, maximum braking while keeping directional control, and clear the runway. Then find the cause on the ground. Here it was full rich at a high field.

Saturday, 2:30, Claire's Subaru pulled up by the hangar. Ellie was out before it stopped. Shorts, soccer cleats (lucky, she said, they'd won twice in them), and Danny's old Hangar Six cap, on the last hole and still down over her eyebrows. Booster cushion under one arm. Claire had left the soft cooler of waters in the Subaru, and she had the face of somebody who'd talked herself into this for the whole drive up from Parker.
At three the ATIS said thirty five degrees, altimeter two niner eight two, wind variable at four. Jordan had the worksheet from Thursday on a clipboard. Two lines were blank.
Your worksheet, Abby said. How are you getting their numbers?
Against the hangar wall sat Marisol's big flat scale on casters. Parts, luggage, and one time, for reasons nobody would explain to Jordan, a goat.
Two lines on the worksheet are blank, for Claire and Ellie. How should Jordan fill them?
A. Weigh Claire and Ellie on Marisol's scale, dressed to fly.
B. Write in 170 for Claire and 80 for Ellie. Close enough for a lap.
C. Leave them blank. She's sure four people won't reach max gross.
D. Ask Claire and Ellie their weights, and add five pounds to each.

Ellie thinks the airplane scale is the best thing that's happened all summer. 76 in cleats and the cap. Booster, 3. Claire gets on, gets off, says nothing. Abby, 150, as advertised. Jordan, 162 in boots. Bags and water, 20. Pencil, blank lines, done. From the bench Marisol says, mostly to the carburetor, First time anybody's used that thing for the airplane.

Exactly right. At the edge of the envelope, real weights matter. Weighing people as they'll fly, with shoes and gear, and weighing the baggage removes the guesswork. The PHAK says standard weights shouldn't be used when actual weights are available.

She did the worksheet on the hood of Claire's Subaru. The briefing room was a hundred yards off and losing its own fight with the heat. Everybody stood there and watched her, and she hated it. Pencil. One line, then the next. No talking. Like charting a code after.

Biscuit's weight and balance for Saturday, August 15, at three. The total is 2,311 pounds at a CG of 44.19, and the max is 2,300, so she's over by eleven. Without the bags and the water it's 2,291, nine under. Pressure altitude 5,985, density altitude about 9,820. From the 2,300 pound block, the six thousand foot row at 35 degrees, no wind: 1,443 feet of ground roll and 2,655 to clear fifty feet, and a climb of about 410 feet a minute.
She went back to the top and added it again. Same number. Of course.
Talk me through it, Abby said. She wasn't going to make the call. She'd said so Tuesday night, more or less, and she meant it.

We're eleven over. If we leave every bag and the water on the ramp, we're nine under. Nine pounds. On the hottest day this summer, at almost ten thousand feet of density altitude, which is the worst Biscuit can do. Four hundred feet a minute up, through the bumps, at seventy five hundred, which is sixteen hundred feet over Parker with the cumulus going up. She heard herself and kept going. The runway's fine. The runway isn't the problem. It's legal by nine pounds and a jug of water, and I'd be doing it because it's legal.
Nobody said anything. Out on the ramp the heat came up off the concrete in sheets and made the hangars across the way wobble. Somewhere a Cirrus was doing its run up and it sounded tired too.

I'd fly it, Abby said, finally. Legally. I've flown worse. And I'd spend the whole climb with my hand next to the throttle, wishing I'd said no in the parking lot. She looked at Jordan. Your numbers. Your call.
Jordan wrote one more line at the bottom of the sheet.
September, seven in the morning, fourteen degrees, thirty ten, twenty gallons: 2,191 pounds with bags, CG 43.98, density altitude about 6,950.
She'd worked it out last night, in case, and hadn't told anybody, because doing the math for the no felt like deciding it.
Then she crouched down in front of Ellie, on the hot concrete, so they were eye to eye under the brim of the cap.
Ellie looked at her, then at the airplane, then at her mother, then back. She'd measured herself on the pantry door. She'd worn her lucky cleats. But it's legal. You said.

It's legal. Barely. You know how Biscuit gets out of breath when it's hot? Today she'd be out of breath with all four of us and the gas, the whole way up. I don't want your first time to be her worst day. I want it to be her best one.
Your dad promised when you were tall enough. You're tall enough. It's the airplane that isn't ready today.

It didn't help. Ellie's chin went first. Jordan had seen that on a lot of kids in the back of the rig. Then Ellie was crying, hard, and Danny's cap fell off on the concrete, and she stepped on it with a cleat and didn't notice. Claire picked her up. Ellie was too big to carry and Claire carried her anyway, and looked at Jordan over Ellie's head.

Jordan expected anger. She'd have understood it. What she got was a nod. Small. The same one Claire gave doctors in the ER, Jordan figured, when they said the thing nobody wanted to hear and said it right.
Later Jordan would think about how easy it would have been to guess. Four people in a 172, a kid, a lap around the airport. Every guess she could have made would have been a little light.

Claire carried Ellie to the car and sat in the back seat with her with the door open and the engine running for the air. Abby went inside without saying anything, which was the kindest thing anyone did all afternoon. Marisol put the scale back against the wall and put the booster cushion on top of it, carefully, like it was going to be needed.

Jordan walked out to Biscuit. She took the sunshade down and opened the door and sat in the left seat with the door open, the vinyl hot enough through her jeans to make her jump. By the mag switch, Ellie's sticker: HI DAD, in purple marker, the corners curling up in the heat. She took the green notebook out of her bag. She'd been reading it in order, mostly. She didn't do that today. She went looking for August, and found it.

Danny's logbook, a page from August, ten years ago. August 28. KAPA local, rental 172 from the school, 0.6. 94 degrees. Me, Claire, Tomás and Bree from Claire's work in back, full tanks, cooler in the baggage, because we were going to fly over Cherry Creek at sunset and it was going to be great. Walt was at the fuel truck and asked what we weighed. I said "not much." Ha. Asked for 28 because it was right there. Used most of it. MOST OF IT. 4,800 feet and the wheels came off somewhere past where I could see the end, and then she just hung there over the fence and thought about it. Climbed like a shopping cart. Took forever to get to pattern altitude. Claire held my knee the whole time and didn't say anything, which was worse than yelling. Back on the ground I did the math I should have done before. Over gross. Didn't lean either. New rule: W&B on paper every time there's more than two of us. If it's hot, do it twice. Claire says don't write down that she was there because she's not sure she was supposed to be flying. I said I don't write anything down. (+1 aboard. She doesn't know I know. Due in April.)
Jordan read it twice, and then a third time on the last line, and then she sat with her hand flat on the page for a long time.

Ten years ago in August. Due in April. Ellie had been in the back of an overloaded 172 on a 94 degree day, hanging over the fence on runway 28, before she was anybody. Before Danny was anybody's dad. He'd known. He'd written it in parentheses.

The right door opened. Claire, folding herself in like the seat might bite. She pulled the door to but didn't latch it. Red eyes, dry now. Out cold. Cried herself to sleep in the back seat. Marisol's in the car with her, doing a crossword out loud. She looked at the notebook. Which one's that?
Jordan handed it over, open. Claire read. Jordan could tell exactly when she hit the parentheses. Hand over the mouth, like at the lawyer's office in April. Then down again.

He knew, she said. I hadn't told him. I had a card picked out. The short laugh. I remember that fence. I didn't get in one for ten years. Today was going to be the first time. He wrote that rule. I never saw him do it on the hood of a car. She held the notebook on her knees with both hands. He'd have taken her today. It probably would've been fine.

Probably fine. We chart that at work. It's not a vital sign. She gave the notebook back. September, seven AM. I read the bottom of your sheet. She got out, then leaned back in with one hand on the roof. Bring the scale.
At 9:40 that night, in Aurora, the phone buzzed twice in a row.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Claire told me. You told the baby no. Good. I am proud of you mija. I am still not getting in that airplane.
A text from Abby Strand. Right call. Next is pattern work. Crosswinds, go arounds, slips, and you landing it every time. Walt says he's coming to watch. Ignore him. You won't be able to.

She read both of them standing at the counter in her socks. Then she got the legal pad out of her bag, turned to a clean page, and wrote SEPTEMBER at the top of it, and under that, in her own small handwriting, the weights she'd measured that afternoon, every one of them, so she wouldn't have to ask anybody again.
